8. His next submission is that the prosecution has not produced the material and independent witnesses who are cited in the charge-sheet as witnesses to prove the prosecution case and such the trial Court ought to have drawn adverse presumption against the genuineness of the case and the accused appellant ought to have been given benefit of doubt and acquitted and lastly his submission is that in the facts and circumstances of the case, the sentence is too severe. 

 17. Now, from an analysis of the entire evidence on record it is now only P.W.1 who stands as the solitary witness to prove the prosecution case beyond all reasonable doubt. Admittedly he is the informant as well as the Investigating Officer in the case and naturally he is an interested witness. Apart form that his evidence as discussed above suffers from serious infirmity and he has not been corroborated by any independent and disinterested witness in material particulars. In a case under section 19(A) and (f) of the Arms Act read with section 3 of the Special Powers Act the prosecution has to establish accused's possession and effective control over the alleged unauthorised arms and ammunitions by cogent and reliable evidence beyond all reasonable doubt. In the instant case, it does not appear to be so established by the prosecution. Thus the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant that it is a case of no evidence, appears to have much force and as such we are unable to uphold the order of conviction and sentence passed against the appellant. Apart from that, non-production of some material witnesses particularly the witnesses who were named in the charge-sheet and alleged to have accompanied the informant to the place of occurrence and witnessed the alleged recovery of the alleged arms and ammunitions naturally gives rise to an adverse presumption against the genuineness of the prosecution case. It is true that even if a single witness, if believed by the court, the conviction can be upheld in view of section 134 of the Evidence Act, but in such a case that single witness must be of such a quality that he or she can be wholly reliable. In the instant case as we have discussed above, the informant P.W.1 is the only witness left to establish the charge against the accused appellant, but his evidence is not of that quality as required to be relied upon without sufficient corroboration.
